jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: The Final Markdown
jokes.joke: My girlfriend dumped me, and two days later I found the sweater I gave her at a thrift store. Five bucks. I paid eighty. I bought it back out of spite. The cashier said, 'No returns.' I said, 'Believe me, I've heard.'

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Resale Value
jokes.joke: My ex moved on so fast that I found out at the thrift store. Her new boyfriend was wearing my old jacket. I donated it during the breakup. He looked great in it, too, which really hurt. Even worse, the tag said $6. She didn't just replace me, she replaced me at a markdown, and he came with better pockets.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Clearance Rack Romance
jokes.joke: I knew my ex was completely over me when I found the custom photo mug I gave her for our anniversary at the local thrift store. Honestly, the donation wasn't what destroyed my ego. It was seeing a fifty-cent sticker right over my face. And it had a red tag. Meaning it had been there for a month, it was on clearance, and even strangers looking for a cheap pencil holder wanted absolutely nothing to do with our relationship.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Blame the Previous Owner
jokes.joke: I'm so insecure about my style that I only shop at thrift stores. That way if the clothes look terrible, it's not on me—it's on the last guy who wore them. Last week I found a blazer with a faded name tag still sewn in: Brad. Now when people stare I just shrug and say, "Talk to Brad. He's the one with the questionable taste. I'm just the current host body."

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Used Confidence
jokes.joke: I'm so insecure I tried to save money on self-esteem at a thrift store. I found a jacket that made me look confident, but every time I wore it, strangers would walk up and say, 'Oh wow, that's mine!' Nothing crushes your confidence faster than finding out your personality has had three previous owners.

scores.comment: Clear premise and natural first-person delivery. The markdown metaphor earns a mild laugh, but the better-pockets tag feels arbitrary and weakens the finish.
The fifty-cent sticker covering the narrator's face is a strong, concrete comic image. The clearance escalation adds humor, but the lengthy explanation dilutes the final punch.
Understandable premise with a mildly amusing transfer of blame to Brad. The host-body ending sounds more quirky than funny, and the joke lacks a strong final turn.

Economical construction, clear escalation, and a coherent final metaphor. The previous-owners punchline fits the premise neatly, although the underlying joke about secondhand confidence is fairly predictable.
Clear premise and tight escalation. The spite buyback sets up the ‘No returns’ reversal, and the last line lands on a double meaning. Familiar breakup-gift territory, but cleanly built.

The sticker over his face and the red tag are good images. The ending is a long explanatory sentence that spells out the joke, and the ‘donation wasn’t what destroyed my ego’ line is clumsy, so the laugh gets diluted.
Blame-shifting to the previous owner is a real comic idea, and the Brad name tag is a good concrete detail. ‘Current host body’ is a fun closer, though the setup logic is slightly strained.

‘Personality has had three previous owners’ is a strong closing line. The middle is muddled, because strangers each claiming the jacket is theirs doesn’t cleanly escalate, and the opening ‘save money on self-esteem’ is a little forced.
Tight stage rhythm with a satisfying, double-meaning punchline that perfectly matches the breakup context.
'Replaced me at a markdown' is a strong turn, but the physical logic of seeing the price tag on a jacket the new boyfriend is actively wearing muddles the imagery.
Excellent escalation. 'I'm just the current host body' is a highly effective, unexpected, and memorable closing punchline.
The final thought about a pre-owned personality is conceptually sharp, but the setup relies on a highly artificial scenario to get there.
Tight spite-to-rejection callback; clean stage rhythm and final snap.
Solid markdown and pockets escalation; effective but slightly padded.
Clearance and pencil-holder details land; a touch explanatory.
Personality-owners metaphor is neat; mild payoff after the setup.
Strong concise setup-to-punch structure. The cashier line is a clean, relatable reversal that lands hard.
Clear premise with some escalation, but the markdown/replacement angle is fairly familiar and the ending is weaker.
Good specificity and escalation. The clearance-tag detail adds texture, though the final image is more amusing than laugh-out-loud.
Solid character voice and clear premise. 'Current host body' is a fun twist, but it leans quirky more than strongly funny.
